title: Resolving Circular Dependencies
content: As the system grew, the method of passing data (prop-drilling) was becoming a maintenance nightmare. My goal was to move from a "scripted" terminal to a true Global OS State. I wanted a centralized system where any component—whether it’s a could interact with the OS without needing to know the complex logic behind it. Right now, a command would have to run down multiple files to do a singular task.

The biggest hurdle was State Fragmentation. My Virtual File System (VFS) was static, and my command logic was "dirty" meaning commands were directly reaching out to change the UI state. This created a massive synchronization issue: if a user created a file in Vim, the ls command didn't know it existed because it was looking at a hard-coded file instead of a live state. We were also teetering on the edge of "Circular Dependencies," where files were importing each other in an infinite loop that would eventually crash the build.

The Global Terminal Context: I implemented a TerminalProvider using the React Context API. This acts as the "Central Engine," holding the CWD, command history, and the VFS in a single source of truth. Now, components just "hook" into the OS to get DIRECTLY what they need.

The Pure Command Pattern: I refactored the command_processor into a pure logic engine. Instead of commands directly changing the directory or deleting files, they now return a "Packet of Intent" (a CommandResponse). The Engine reads this packet and executes the state mutation safely, decoupling the logic from the UI.

Stateful VFS & Session RAM: I moved the entire file system into React state. By merging the static "System Files" with a volatile "Session RAM," the environment now reacts in real-time. When you save a file in the editor or delete a log, the DirectoryExplorer updates instantly because it’s observing the live state.

The architecture is now no longer holds a circular dependency. By enforcing strict TypeScript interfaces and a decoupled data flow, the system is now easier to extend if any future features were to be added.

title: Grabbing Data And Planning
content: # Update: Architecting the EV Draft Predictor and Overhauling the ETL Pipeline
- I've lowkey been working on this for a hot minute now but just haven't been updating this blog.

- To catch up though, the previous model I built achieving an **ROC-AUC of 0.56**. While this was a decent model for a game like League Of Legends. It still lacked in some areas where I could not fix with the given data.

- I was collecting data at the end of the game, but this was a **massive oversight**. Why? Because of **target leakage** I was trying to predict which was a winning draft based on a team that was already **winning**. This affected some data like damage_per_minute and self_mitigated_damage because the winning team would have higher level meaning higher stats and more gold meaning, once again, higher stats.
- This was a major setback (two weeks worth of work) as collecting data with the limited developer API takes forever!!
- **TLDR: Winning team typically wins more therefore data trying to predict a draft using winning team data would be slightly flawed.**
- **Status**: Backend Extraction Created and Collecting Data

Shifting the League of Legends draft tool from a **descriptive model** (which just looked at final game stats and resulted in a flawed ROC-AUC) to a predictive **Expected Value (EV) model**. The goal is to train and build an AI that evaluates team chemistry and lane matchups while also adhearing to the information we have during drafting phase (unknown position of enemies and flex picks)

I needed to fundamentally change what data was being collected. Instead of just grabbing final damage and gold, I wanted to capture early-game milestones (15, 20, 25, 30 mins) to map out champion power curves, while isolating specific combat stats to mathematically define champion identities (Engage, Peel, Drain Tank, etc.) without human bias. I will attempt to do this using K-Means-Clustering.

Target Leakage: The old approach essentially gave the AI the final score of the game and asked it to predict who won. It didn't teach the model how to draft. While this was good enough, I wanted something better.

The Flex Pick Problem: Evaluating a draft is incredibly difficult when the enemy picks a champion like Sylas or Malphite early on, as their role and build (AP vs. Tank) are completely hidden until later in the draft. This creates a lot of nuance when it comes for our model to predict who we should suggest.

Riot API Limitations: The Riot Timeline API is purely an economic ledger; it doesn't track running utility stats like Crowd Control or Healing. This means we would have to do 3 total API calls to Riot which is quite expensive for a lone developer to do. Furthermore, League's XP curve is non-linear. If a game ended at 23 minutes, simply guessing the 25-minute XP based on their champion level created massive mathematical errors that would ruin the baseline data.

Production Stability: I need so much data, but the developer key allows for, at most, 100 requests every 2 minutes. Which is `720 * 100 = 72,000` requests a day, but each match takes 3 calls to process. 1 to grab the match_id, and 2 to both the Riot endgame API and the Timeline API. Which is at most `24,000` matches a day.
The Architecture: The data extraction was split to feed two distinct systems.

**Identity Engine:** Pulls end-game Match-V5 data (Mitigation ratios, True Damage Share, Healing Volume, Ally Healing) to eventually feed an unsupervised K-Means clustering algorithm. This will automatically group champions into distinct 5v5 archetypes. **[*HOPEFULLY*]**
**Prediction Engine:** Pulls exact Gold, XP, and CS from the Timeline API at specific milestones to calculate historical Expected Value (EV) for lane matchups and 2v2 synergies.

**Dynamic Counter Logic**: To handle flex picks, the architecture was designed to utilize a Global_Counter matrix for unknown enemy picks, which instantly transitions to a highly specific Lane_Counter we know for sure where the enemy is going.

**Python Workers:** The worker.py script was completely rewritten. It now features safe math floors, a clean batch-logging system to reduce terminal clutter, and fallback logic for games that end early (grabbing the literal final frame of the game)
**Zero-Downtime Migration & Network Resiliency:** A brand new match_participants_v2 Supabase table was created to house the new schema without breaking the legacy infrastructure.

A fully automated ETL backend that silently and efficiently chews through thousands of Riot API requests. The database is now actively populating with mathematically sound data that tracks both economic power curves and 5v5 combat identities, completely eliminating target leakage and perfectly setting the stage for training the new XGBoost draft model.

title: Clickable Ui Navigation
content: While terminal interfaces are fun for engineers, internal-beta testing (aka asking my non-tech friends) revealed they are incredibly difficult for non-technical users to navigate. My goal was to completely remove the learning curve without losing the terminal aesthetic.

A terminal relies on a user typing exact text commands based on their "Current Working Directory." Allowing users to simply click a file that exists in a completely different folder confused the system, as it didn't know how to route them back to the root folder to open it. This was a major issue since if the user ever decided to scroll up and click on another directory or file. It may pop a does not exist error. The file system laid out was great for a command-line based navigation, but was not not designed for clickable navigation in mind.

* **Interactive DOM Injection:** I converted the static text outputs into an interactive interface. Now, all text files, project folders, and executables render as clickable buttons that silently run the correct terminal commands in the background.

* **Absolute Path Engine:** Instead of a button simply firing a command like `cat [filename]`, the DirectoryExplorer component now calculates the absolute path of every file. `path_resolver` joins the directory + the filename giving something like `/` + `about.txt` = `/about.txt`. Now when the button is pressed it will output `cat /about.txt`

Non-technical visitors and recruiters can now explore the entire operating system using just their mouse—identical to a standard website experience. While more technical users can still type raw commands if they choose to do so.

title: Code Refactor And Mobile
content: As the project scaled up, the underlying code became massive and difficult to manage. The goal was to optimize the site's architecture for speed and future growth, while also fixing layout issues that were frustrating mobile users.

The site's "navigation" logic was highly repetitive, which left room for bugs when users tried to jump between multiple folders at once. Furthermore, the desktop-focused design was stretching horizontally on phone screens, breaking the immersion.
* **Modular Architecture:** I completely dismantled the monolithic codebase and separated the file system, commands, and text documents into distinct, modular pieces.
* **Centralized Navigation:** I engineered a single "Path Resolver" tool. Instead of each command guessing where a file is, they all share one highly accurate map of the site's architecture.
* **Mobile Overhaul:** I ensured the stretching was no longer an issue on mobile and ensured that if the user on mobile were to type. The view would not be destroyed by the keyboard rising
A cleaner product that resolved some bugs that may get users stuck, and mobile users can now also enjoy the website!
